title: Electrical sensor and AI could help detect extraterrestrial life
byline: Cult of MacFollowAnurag ChawakeMon, October 5, 2026 at 11:00 PM UTCAdd us on Google
excerpt: Japanese researchers built an electrical sensor that reads single molecules, a step toward compact tools that detect extraterrestrial life.
content:
A new electrical technique could someday help space missions detect alien life by telling mirror-image molecules apart.

The sensor pairs a tiny gold gap with AI to read molecules one at a time. It needs no optical measurements or chiral recognition molecules.

Molecular handedness could help detect extraterrestrial life

Researchers at the University of Osaka in Japan built the sensor, and they detailed it in Nature Communications on Monday.

The target is amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. Each one comes in two mirror-image forms, called L and D.

Life on Earth almost exclusively uses the L-form. Nonliving chemistry makes both forms in equal amounts, so a lopsided L-to-D ratio is a potential biosignature of life.

Standard lab methods usually measure large groups of molecules at once. Electrical detection, the team says, could be simpler and less sensitive to vibration.

Single molecules leave an electrical fingerprint

The sensor uses the gap between two gold nanowires, roughly half a nanometer wide. When an amino acid passes through it, it creates a tiny spike in electrical current. L- and D- forms produce different waveforms.

A machine-learning algorithm then tells them apart. The team then distinguished individual L- and D- amino acids with more than 80% accuracy.

Lead author Takahito Ohshiro said the work is "the first discrimination of amino-acid chirality at the single-molecule level."

And because the sensor counts molecules one by one, it can also estimate the ratio of L to D forms, and handle simple mixtures too. Mixtures of four amino acids with different chiral makeups were quantified with more than 66% accuracy.

Meteorite and desert soil put the sensor to the test

Real samples are, of course, messier than lab standards. So the team tested extracts from the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia, and desert soil from two places in Chile's Atacama Desert. Another site, north of Antofagasta, is a Mars-analog environment.

Researchers said they checked results against liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, a standard reference method. The nanogap readings then captured the major features of the amino acid mix in the samples.

Space missions are still a long way off

Don't expect this on a rover anytime in the near future. The method is apparently a targeted approach, not a full chemical profile.

The test targeted 11 species, and results varied by amino acid and by sample. While some measurements matched the reference method, others did not. In both desert soils, glutamic acid was not retained.

The authors say practical use will need further validation under contamination. But there's a hardware upside. The chip's materials tolerate temperatures above 300 degrees Celsius (572 degrees Fahrenheit), meaning it could travel without cooling. The approach is also compact and works without chemical reagents.

Even then, a lopsided ratio could be a clue. But a compact electrical sensor could give future missions sharper tools in the search for life.
